etymology: From louse (Old English lūs), plural lice. Lousy meant literally "infested with lice" in Middle English, and was already a term of contempt for a mean or vile person by the late 1300s. The broad slang sense — poor, rotten, inferior, miserable ("a lousy meal," "I feel lousy") — spread in American speech in the early 20th century and was carried everywhere by the soldiers of both World Wars, who knew the literal sense from the trenches and the barracks. By the 1940s and 1950s it was the everyday complaint word of the Silent Generation, and "lousy with" (swarming with: "the town was lousy with cops") rode along beside it.
biblical_def: When your grandfather was a boy, lousy was the all-purpose word for anything that disappointed him: a lousy movie, lousy weather, a lousy hand of cards, a lousy day at the plant. The men who came home from the war had earned the word honestly — they had lived with real lice in foxholes and troopships, and everything bad after that was simply lousy. The word is not filthy, and a grandparent who used it was not sinning by the word itself. But it is worth noticing what the word is usually for. It is the word of the complaint. Israel in the wilderness had a lousy word for the manna too: "our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes" (Num 11:6), and Scripture records that "when the people complained, it displeased the LORD" (Num 11:1). God once sent real lice on Egypt as a judgment (Exo 8:17), and the Christian who calls every small trouble "lousy" is in danger of treating ordinary providence as if it were a plague. Paul, who had been beaten, shipwrecked, and jailed, wrote instead, "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Php 4:11), and commanded the church, "Do all things without murmurings and disputings" (Php 2:14). That contentment is not a stiff upper lip; it is the fruit of knowing Christ, who has given us Himself, so that "in every thing" we can "give thanks" (1Th 5:18). A lousy day in the hands of a good Father is never only lousy.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (from Middle English "full of lice"; broadened by two World Wars) for poor, rotten, miserable — the everyday word of complaint, which Scripture answers with contentment and thanks in every thing (Php 4:11).
webster_full: LOUSY, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1910s–50s; GI staple of both World Wars) Poor, inferior, rotten; miserable or ill. "What a lousy break." "I feel lousy today." Also lousy with: swarming with, full of.
Webster (1828) — LOUS’Y, adjective s as z. [louse.] 1. Swarming with lice; infested with lice. 2. Mean; low; contemptible; as a lousy knave.
Decode for families: when Grandpa says "lousy," he means bad; the old literal meaning (crawling with lice) is why the word sounded so strong.
scriptures: Num 11:1

And when the people complained, it displeased the LORD: and the LORD heard it; and his anger was kindled; and the fire of the LORD burnt among them, and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp.
Exo 8:17

And they did so; for Aaron stretched out his hand with his rod, and smote the dust of the earth, and it became lice in man, and in beast; all the dust of the land became lice throughout all the land of Egypt.
Php 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
Php 2:14
Do all things without murmurings and disputings:
In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.
corruption_summary: A plain, unprofane word whose only danger is its use: it is the natural vocabulary of grumbling, and Scripture calls the believer from murmuring to contentment and thanks.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with saying a meal was lousy when it was. Honest description is not sin. The trouble is the habit the word feeds. A family can fall into a rhythm in which every day, every teacher, every boss, and every Sunday sermon is lousy, and that rhythm is the murmuring that Israel practised in the wilderness. God heard it as complaint against Himself, because it was: the manna they called worthless was His daily gift (Num 11:1).

The cure is not a ban on the word but a change of heart. Paul learned contentment "in whatsoever state" (Php 4:11) because his state was in Christ’s hands. A grandparent who once called the whole Depression lousy and then thanked God at supper for beans and bread was teaching the right lesson, whatever word he used.
roots_summary: Old English lūs (louse) → Middle English lousy (full of lice; vile) → early 20th c. American slang (poor, rotten) → WWI–WWII GI usage → Silent Generation everyday complaint word.
roots_lines: Middle English lousy — infested with lice; by extension mean, vile, contemptible
Early 20th c. American slang: lousy — poor, inferior, miserable
WWI and WWII: soldiers’ staple word, from the real lice of trench and barracks
usage: "Lousy weather for a ball game," Grandpa said, and then he went and dug out the board games instead.
I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content (Php 4:11).
Do all things without murmurings and disputings (Php 2:14).

etymology: American, recorded from the 1930s. The usual explanation comes from radio broadcasting: a producer in the control booth signalled the people on the air that the program was running exactly on time by touching a finger to the side of his nose. The phrase spread from radio to everyday speech in the 1940s and 1950s for anything exactly right, precise, or punctual ("nine o’clock on the nose"). The same years also had a horse-racing sense: a bet "on the nose" is a bet that a horse will win outright, not place or show.
biblical_def: To your grandparents’ generation, on the nose meant exactly right. Dinner at six on the nose. A guess on the nose. A carpenter who cut a board on the nose did not need to cut it twice. It came out of the radio age, when a whole country set its clocks by a program that had to start on the second, and it carries a respect for exactness that belongs to that generation — men who built ships, bridges, and bombers to tolerances, and women who balanced the household books to the penny. Scripture honours that kind of exactness, because God Himself is exact. "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" (Pro 11:1). "A just weight and balance are the LORD’S" (Pro 16:11). Our Lord taught that our speech should be on the nose too: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil" (Mat 5:37). And the Christian minister is to handle the Bible with the same care, "rightly dividing the word of truth" (2Ti 2:15). The greatest "on the nose" in history is the coming of Christ: "when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son" (Gal 4:4) — not a day early, not a day late. The God who keeps His appointments to the second is the God who keeps His promises.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1930s radio, from a producer’s on-time signal) for exactly right, precise, punctual — a love of exactness that answers to the God whose just weight is his delight (Pro 11:1).
webster_full: ON THE NOSE, phrase (Silent Generation slang, 1930s–50s; from radio broadcasting) Exactly; precisely; on time to the second. "The bus came at eight on the nose." "Your guess was right on the nose." In racing, a bet on the nose is a bet to win.
Decode for families: it means exactly right. If Grandpa says you’re home "nine on the nose," he is pleased.
scriptures: Pro 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
A just weight and balance are the LORD'S: all the weights of the bag are his work.
Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
corruption_summary: A wholesome word of exactness; the only caution is its racetrack cousin, the bet "on the nose," which a Christian family can leave at the track.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in the main sense. Exactness in work, in time, and in speech is a Christian virtue, and the phrase is a small monument to a generation that prized it. A workman "that needeth not to be ashamed" (2Ti 2:15) is one whose work comes out on the nose.

The second sense, a bet to win, belongs to the betting window. Grandparents who knew the phrase from the racing page knew where it came from. Scripture’s word on the love of easy money is plain, and a family can enjoy the phrase for punctuality while keeping it far from the wager.
roots_summary: Old English nosu (nose) → 1930s American radio signal (finger to nose = on time) → 1940s–50s everyday slang for exactly right → racing "on the nose" (to win).
roots_lines: 1930s American radio: a producer touching his nose signals the program is exactly on schedule
Racing usage: a bet on the nose — to win outright
usage: "Supper’s at six on the nose, and your grandmother doesn’t hold the gravy."
A just weight and balance are the LORD'S (Pro 16:11).
Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay (Mat 5:37).

etymology: American, first recorded in 1861 among Union soldiers in the opening year of the Civil War, used of troops retreating in a hurry; origin uncertain (fanciful explanations from Greek or Scots dialect are unproven). The word outlived the war as comic, mock-grand slang for leaving fast, and it was the grandparents’ word for it all through the twentieth century: "Now skedaddle!" to children underfoot in the 1930s, 1940s, and 1950s. The Silent Generation did not coin it, but they are the generation that handed it down to the rest of us.
biblical_def: When your grandmother wanted the kitchen clear, she said, "Skedaddle!" and every grandchild scattered. The word is a funny one on purpose, an old soldiers’ joke about running away, and it has always carried a smile. But Scripture has a good deal to say about running, and it sorts the running into two kinds. There is the flight of the guilty: "The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion" (Pro 28:1). That is the skedaddle of Adam hiding in the garden, of Jonah bolting for Tarshish, of the disciples scattering at Gethsemane. And there is the flight of the wise. Joseph, when Potiphar’s wife caught his coat, "left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out" (Gen 39:12) — the most honourable skedaddle in the Bible. Paul tells a young man, "Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace" (2Ti 2:22). James promises that when we stand our ground with God, the enemy is the one who runs: "Resist the devil, and he will flee from you" (Jas 4:7). So the word can teach a child something true. There are things a Christian never runs from: duty, the truth, the cross. And there are things a Christian runs from fast, without stopping to argue. Christ did not skedaddle from Calvary; because He stood, we can flee to Him.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (Union soldiers’ word of 1861, handed down by the grandparents) for leaving in a hurry — and Scripture sorts running two ways: the wicked flee when no man pursueth, the wise flee youthful lusts (2Ti 2:22).
webster_full: SKEDADDLE, v. i. (American slang, 1861; grandparents’ household word through the 20th c.) To run away in haste; to scatter; to clear out. "Go on, skedaddle!"
Decode for families: it means "scram, get going, clear out" — usually said with a grin.
scriptures: Pro 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
And she caught him by his garment, saying, Lie with me: and he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.
Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
Jas 4:7
Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
corruption_summary: A harmless comic word for hurrying off; Scripture uses it to ask which way we run: from duty like the guilty, or from temptation like Joseph.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no harm in the word. It is a family joke older than anyone now living, and it is usually said kindly. The lesson it opens is about the direction of our running. The wicked flee "when no man pursueth" (Pro 28:1), because a guilty conscience is its own pursuer.

A Christian child should learn to skedaddle at the right times: from the dirty joke, the party that has turned, the screen that should be shut. Joseph did not debate with temptation; "he left his garment in her hand, and fled" (Gen 39:12). That is the kind of running the Bible commends.
roots_summary: Origin uncertain → 1861 Union army slang for a hasty retreat → late 19th c. comic American word for running off → 20th c. grandparents’ household word ("Now skedaddle!").
roots_lines: Origin uncertain; proposed Greek and Scots-dialect sources are unproven
1861: recorded among Union soldiers for troops retreating in haste
Late 19th c.: general comic slang for running away, clearing out
20th c.: the grandparents’ word to scatter children from the kitchen
usage: "Supper’s in ten minutes — now skedaddle and wash those hands."
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion (Pro 28:1).

etymology: A 20th-century American variant of the older English smouch (a loud kiss; to kiss), recorded from the 16th century and probably imitative of the sound. Smooch in this spelling is recorded from the 1930s and became the everyday light-hearted word for a kiss in the 1940s and 1950s — the word of the war-bride letters, the movie-magazine columns, and the front porch. It has never lost its playful tone: a smooch is affectionate, not passionate.
biblical_def: A smooch was what Grandpa gave Grandma in the kitchen when he came home from work, and what a soldier wrote he was saving for his girl when the war was over. It is a light word for a good thing. Scripture is not embarrassed by kisses. The Song of Solomon opens with one: "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better than wine" (Son 1:2) — married love, honoured by God and sung in His Book. The early church greeted one another with a kiss, and Paul made it holy: "Salute one another with an holy kiss" (Rom 16:16). But Scripture also knows that a kiss can lie. "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (Pro 27:6), and the darkest kiss in history was in a garden: "Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?" (Luk 22:48). So a grandfather can teach two things with this word. First, affection is good, and a home where husbands and wives and grandparents and grandchildren hug and kiss is a home that reflects the love of God. Second, a kiss means something, and it should be given only where it is true and in its proper place. To young people Scripture says gently, "stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Son 2:7). Kisses are meant to be honest — like the love of Christ, who never kissed and betrayed.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1930s American, from 16th-century smouch) for a light, affectionate kiss — and Scripture both honours the kiss of true love (Son 1:2) and warns that the kisses of an enemy are deceitful (Pro 27:6).
webster_full: SMOOCH, v. i. and n. (Silent Generation slang, 1930s–50s; variant of smouch) To kiss; a kiss, especially a light or affectionate one. "Give your grandmother a smooch."
Webster (1828) — SMOUCH, verb transitive To salute. [Not in use.] (Webster’s "salute" here means to greet with a kiss.)
Decode for families: a smooch is a friendly kiss — Grandma’s word for the peck on the cheek.
scriptures: Son 1:2
Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better than wine.
Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you.
Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
But Jesus said unto him, Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?
Son 2:7
I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.
corruption_summary: A sweet, playful word for a kiss; its only shadow is the culture’s habit of making kisses cheap, where Scripture keeps them true and in their place.
corruption_paragraphs: The word itself is innocent; the 1940s used it of the kiss a husband gave his wife and a grandmother gave a grandchild. What changed after the Silent Generation’s youth is how lightly kisses came to be given. A kiss that means nothing teaches a heart that affection means nothing, and the Song of Solomon warns young people not to stir love up before its time (Son 2:7).

Scripture’s highest word on kisses is that they must be honest. The holy kiss of the church (Rom 16:16) was a sign of real love in Christ; the kiss of Judas was a sign used to betray Him (Luk 22:48). A Christian family can keep the warm kiss at home and teach its children that a kiss is a promise, not a game.
roots_summary: Imitative 16th-c. English smouch (a kiss) → 1930s American smooch → 1940s–50s everyday playful word for a kiss → still the grandparents’ word.
roots_lines: 16th c. English smouch — a loud kiss; to kiss (probably imitative of the sound)
1940s–50s: the light, affectionate word for a kiss in letters, movies, and magazines
Compare smack (a loud kiss), another imitative word
usage: "Before you go out to play, come give your Grandma a smooch."
Salute one another with an holy kiss (Rom 16:16).
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful (Pro 27:6).
